extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys drafting or prosecuting chemical and biotechnology patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and claim-drafting of chemical and biotechnology inventions, covering claim types, novelty, inventive step, unity, industrial applicability, and deposition/disclosure requirements for biological materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagram explanation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The diagram shall be explained in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any drawing/diagram included in the application must be accompanied by an explanation in the description so that its meaning is clear to the examiner and a person skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative expressions acceptable when clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative written description instead of numeric quantitative expressions is acceptable if it is clear in meaning and known in the relevant field of technology, such as "the content is sufficient to make certain material moistened", "catalytic amount", etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use qualitative terms when they have an established meaning in the relevant technical field; avoid ambiguous qualitative phrases. Such terms are permissible in claims/description provided their meaning is clear to those skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of composition claims (non-defining, function-defining, use-defining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, there are three types of claims of a composition: non-defining, function-defining and use-defining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose claim type based on the disclosure: non-defining claims are permitted when composition has multiple applicable properties/fields; where only one property or use is disclosed, draft as function-defining or use-defining. In certain fields (e.g., alloys) intrinsic property/use usually should be specified. Most pharmaceutical claims shall be drafted as the use-defining type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted characterization by physical/chemical parameters or manufacturing process
rubrics_metrics.description: For a chemical product which cannot be clearly characterized merely by features of structure and/or composition, it is permitted to further use physical/chemical parameter(s) and/or the manufacturing process to characterize the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Use physical/chemical parameters when structure is unclear; parameters must be clear enough. (2) Use manufacturing process to characterize the product only when the product cannot be sufficiently characterized by other features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claim feature categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim of a chemical process may be defined by the features of the process relating to procedure, substance and apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure features include steps and conditions (temperature, pressure, time, catalysts, auxiliaries). Substance features include chemical components, structural formula, and physical/chemical parameter(s) of raw materials and products. Apparatus features include the type of apparatus and its properties/functions related to the process. Select one or more of these feature types depending on subject matter and technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claim is a process claim (distinguishing wording)
rubrics_metrics.description: A use invention is an invention of process; its claim is a process claim. Wording such as "using compound X as an insecticide" indicates a use (process) claim, whereas "an insecticide made of compound X" is a product claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must take notice of wording to distinguish use claims from product claims. Do not construe "use of compound X as an insecticide" as equivalent to "the compound X for an insecticide" (the latter is a product claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical use claim drafting constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: An application relating to the medical use of a substance shall not be granted if its claim is drafted in the wording "use of substance X for the treatment of diseases", "use of substance X for diagnosis of diseases" or "use of substance X as a medicament", because such claim is one for "method for the diagnosis or for the treatment of diseases" (Rule 7(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pharmaceutical or use claims framed as methods for manufacturing a medicament are acceptable, e.g., "use of substance X for the manufacturing of a medicament" or "use of compound X for manufacturing a medicament for the treatment of disease Y". Draft medical-related claims in patentable formats consistent with Rule 7(3) and the Patent Law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of a compound: "refer to" standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If a compound has been referred to in a reference document, it is deduced that the compound does not possess novelty, unless the applicant can provide evidence to verify that the compound is not available before the date of filing. "Refer to" means defined clearly or explained by chemical name, molecular/structural formula, physical/chemical parameter(s) or manufacturing process (including raw materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if name/formula are difficult to identify, disclosure of identifying parameters or an identical manufacturing method can destroy novelty unless applicant proves otherwise. A general formula does not destroy the novelty of a specific compound; disclosure of a specific compound destroys novelty of a general formula only as to that specific compound. A natural substance per se does not destroy novelty unless disclosed and identical or directly equivalent in structure and morphology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of composition defined only by components (consisting of vs containing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment of novelty on a composition merely defined by its components: (i) a claim worded "consisting of A + B" (close-ended) can be novel even if a reference discloses A + B + C; (ii) a claim worded "containing A + B" (open-ended) may lack novelty if reference discloses A + B + C and solves same technical problem; (iii) exclusive manner (indicating that C is not contained) confers novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise claim language (close-ended/exclusive) to preserve novelty where prior art discloses additional components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply Administrative Instruction for compositions by components and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: For judgment of novelty on a composition defined by its components and contents, the provisions of Administrative Instruction 22 shall apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Administrative Instruction 22 when compositions include component amounts/ratios as part of the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty for products characterized by parameters or process
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) If it is impossible to compare the product characterized by physical/chemical parameter(s) with that disclosed in a reference based on the parameters described and to determine their difference, the product claim characterized by said parameter(s) does not possess novelty. (2) For product claims characterized by manufacturing process, novelty shall be determined on the product per se rather than merely comparing processes; a different manufacturing process does not always change the product per se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the only difference from prior art is process without parameters or indications showing change in function/nature, the product claim characterized by process lacks novelty per Section 3(10)(a). Ensure parameters allow meaningful comparison to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of use inventions of chemical products
rubrics_metrics.description: A chemical product that is novel makes a use invention of that product naturally novel. A known product is not rendered novel merely because a new application has been put forward; however, a new use may be patentable as a method if the method per se possesses novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the new use constitutes a distinct method. For medical-use inventions, consider whether the new use differs in substance from known use, whether it is directly revealed by known mechanism/pharmacological action, whether it is only a generic term of a known specific use, and whether distinguishing features merely relate to administration (which do not confer novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for compounds (novel and structurally dissimilar)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a compound is novel, not similar in structure to a known compound, and has a certain use or effect, the examiner may deem it to involve an inventive step without requiring unexpected use or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural dissimilarity combined with a technical effect/use can be sufficient for inventive step; no need for unexpected properties in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for compounds similar to known compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: For a compound similar in structure to a known compound, it must have an unexpected use or effect to involve an inventive step. Unexpected use/effect may be a different use, substantive progress or improvement of a known effect, or an effect not clear in common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether compounds are "similar" depends on the technical field; apply field-dependent criteria. Provide evidence of unexpected technical effect where required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step not denied solely due to structural similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step of a compound ought not to be denied simply on the grounds of structural similarity; it is necessary to further explain that its use or effect can be expected or is predictable, or that a person skilled in the art could produce/use the compound by logical analysis, inference or limited experiment based on prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer obviousness solely from structural similarity; assess predictability and whether routine experiments would lead to the claimed compound/use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious predictable effects negate inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: If the effect of a technical solution is caused by something known and inevitable, the technical solution does not involve an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if prior art indicates increasing alkyl chain length inevitably improves effectiveness, producing the next homolog with improved effect is obvious and lacks inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step of use inventions (new product)
rubrics_metrics.description: A use invention of a new chemical product is regarded as involving an inventive step if the use cannot be expected from the known product having a similar structure or composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess expectations from known similar products; unexpected uses for new products support inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step of use inventions (known product)
rubrics_metrics.description: A use invention of a known product is regarded as involving an inventive step if the new use cannot be derived or expected from the structure, composition, molecular weight, known physical/chemical property and existent use of the product, but utilizes a newly discovered property and produces unexpected technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate the newly discovered property and unexpected technical effect to support inventive step for a new use of a known product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability — dishes and cooking methods
rubrics_metrics.description: A dish which cannot be made industrially and implemented repeatedly does not possess practical applicability, and thus shall not be granted a patent right. A cooking method which depends on uncertain factors such as skills and creativity cannot be implemented repeatedly and thus is not industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must be implementable repeatedly and industrially; avoid claims relying on individual skill/creativity or non-repeatable techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability — medical prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescriptions made by a doctor according to the concrete conditions of a particular patient (and the making up/dispensation merely according to such prescriptions) do not possess practical applicability and shall not be granted patent right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical methods individualized to a patient are not industrially applicable; drafting should target generalizable, repeatable methods or products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Markush (alternative elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush claim (single claim defined by a number of alternative elements) shall comply with unity rules. If alternative elements possess similar nature, they are regarded as technical-related and may meet unity. For Markush elements (alternatives of compounds), unity exists if: (1) all alternatives possess a common property or activity; and (2) all alternatives possess a common structure which constitutes the distinguishing feature and is essential to the common property/activity; or if no common structure, all alternatives belong to the same class of compounds recognized in the technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A "recognized class of compounds" means an expectation from the art that members of the class produce the same intended result and are substitutable. Use concrete examples and explanations to justify unity; lacking common structure or class-recognition may negate unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity absent when alternatives have no common structure or class expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Markush claim lacks unity when alternatives differ in ring size, belong to different heterocycle classes, or include unrelated chemical classes (e.g., inorganic salt, organic acid, amide, nitrile, phenol, amine, heterocycle) without expectation of substitutability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should analyze prior art and technical commonality; diverse chemical classes in alternatives typically fail unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity between intermediate and final product — basic principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity exists between an intermediate and the final product if: (i) the intermediate and the final product have the same basic structure unit, or their chemical structures are technically closely related and the basic structure unit of the intermediate is incorporated into the final product; and (ii) the final product is prepared or separated directly from the intermediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (2) Different processes preparing the same final product from different intermediates may be claimed together if intermediates possess the same basic structure unit. (3) Different intermediates of different structural parts of the same final product shall not be claimed in one application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "biological material" for biotechnology examination
rubrics_metrics.description: "Biological material" means any material containing genetic information and capable of reproducing itself or being reproduced in a biological system, such as gene, plasmid, microorganism, animal, plant, and so on. Definitions of "animal" and "plant" follow Rule 7 bis.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions when determining subject-matter eligibility and applying exclusions in biotechnology-related applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology exclusions under Section 3(3) and Rule 18
rubrics_metrics.description: Some inventions in biotechnology cannot be granted patent right under Section 3(3) and Rule 18, including those listed in Rule 7bis.3 and inventions/creations relying on genetic resources acquired/used not consistent with laws/regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples explicitly unpatentable include embryonic stem cells of human beings and their preparing methods; the human body at various stages of formation and development (germ cell, oosperm, embryo, entire human body); inventions relying on illegally acquired genetic resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 6bis — microorganism patentability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The term "microorganism" includes bacteria, actinomycetes, fungi, viruses, protozoa and algae. A microorganism existing in nature without artificially induced technical treatment is a scientific discovery and unpatentable. A microorganism per se is patentable only when isolated into pure culture and has particular industrial use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation into pure culture plus demonstrated particular industrial use are required for patentability; mere discovery of a natural microorganism is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gene or DNA fragment patentability criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Genes or DNA fragments are, in substance, chemical substances. A gene/DNA fragment found in nature and existing in its natural state is a discovery and unpatentable. However, a gene/DNA fragment per se and the process to obtain it are patentable if it is isolated/extracted for the first time from nature, its base sequence is unknown in the prior art and can be definitely characterized, and it can be exploited industrially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability requires isolation/characterization and industrial applicability; provide sequence data and characterization to support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal/plant subject-matter exclusions and distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryonic stem cells of an animal at various stages of formation/development and single plants and their reproductive material that maintain life by photosynthesis fall into excluded "animal variety"/"plant variety" categories and are unpatentable per Rule 7bis.3/paragraph 3.3.4.1. Somatic cells, tissues and organs of an animal (except embryo) are not in the excluded definition. Cells, tissues and organs of a plant that do not possess the plant-variety characteristic are not excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between varieties and non-variety biological materials; check definitions and Rule 7bis to determine patent eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgenic animals and plants unpatentable per variety exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Transgenic animals or plants obtained by biological methods (e.g., DNA recombination) still belong to the category of "animal variety" or "plant variety" and, in accordance with paragraph 3.3.4.1, no patent right shall be granted to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even genetically modified organisms may fall under the variety exclusions; assess applicability of Rule 7bis and paragraph 3.3.4.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient disclosure — deposit of biological material requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The description shall set forth the invention sufficiently clear and complete so as to enable a person skilled in the art to carry it out (Section 2(9)(b)). In biotechnology, where biological material cannot be fully described or made available, the biological material shall be deposited with a depositary institution designated by the Office according to relevant provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If biological material indispensable for carrying out the invention is not deposited or required deposit certificates are not submitted by filing (or within four months), the examiner shall reject the application for non-compliance. If deposit information was omitted in the description but submitted in the request/certificates on time, the applicant may add deposit information into the description during substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information required when a biological deposit is involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application relates to a biological material not available to the public, it shall indicate in the request and description: the taxonomic denomination and Latin scientific name, the name and address of the depositary institution, the deposit date and the accession number. When first mentioned in the description, add full depositary name and abbreviation, deposit date and accession number as part of the description (position corresponding to drawings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant submitted request and valid deposit certificates on time but omitted deposit details in the description, they may add the relevant information during substantive examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of "biological material not available to the public" and exceptions to deposit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological material not available to the public includes material held privately, deposited with a non-patent-purpose depositary and not released, or material whose production process is described but cannot be repeated by a skilled person. Circumstances where deposit is not required: (i) commercially available material with supplier indicated and evidence of availability before filing; (ii) material deposited with recognized depositary and published/granted before filing; (iii) material disclosed in a non-patent document with public access and proof guaranteeing accessibility for twenty years from filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide documentary evidence when claiming commercial availability or prior deposit/publication. Ensure public accessibility guarantees if relying on non-patent disclosure exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit viability and replacement procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: For biological materials deposited with the depositary institution designated by the Office, the institution shall confirm viability. If the material is confirmed dead, polluted, inactive, or variant, the applicant shall deposit material identical with that initially deposited together with the original sample, notify the Patent Office; the latter deposit is deemed a continuation of the original deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor viability certificates and replace deposits promptly if viability issues arise; notify the Office to maintain compliance with deposit requirements.
